top_cited_works.title: Can face masks offer protection from airborne sneeze and cough droplets in close-up, face-to-face human interactions?—A quantitative study
top_cited_works.abstract: Day-to-day observations reveal numerous medical and social situations where maintaining physical distancing is either not feasible or not practiced during the time of a viral pandemic, such as, the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). During these close-up, face-to-face interactions, a common belief is that a susceptible person wearing a face mask is safe, at least to a large extent, from foreign airborne sneeze and cough droplets. This study, for the first time, quantitatively verifies this notion. Droplet flow visualization experiments of a simulated face-to-face interaction with a mask in place were conducted using the particle image velocimetry setup. Five masks were tested in a snug-fit configuration (i.e., with no leakage around the edges): N-95, surgical, cloth PM 2.5, cloth, and wetted cloth PM 2.5. Except for the N-95 mask, the findings showed leakage of airborne droplets through all the face masks in both the configurations of (1) a susceptible person wearing a mask for protection and (2) a virus carrier wearing a mask to prevent the spreading of the virus. recent_works.title: Mechanisms of Supersonic and Hypersonic Shock Focusing and Attenuation in Particle Arrays: Comparative 2D and 3D Analysis
recent_works.abstract: Shock wave interaction with arrays of solid particles is investigated numerically in the supersonic and hypersonic regime using an open-source compressible solver. A non-staggered 4x4 array of cylinders (2D) or spheres (3D) is subjected to Mach 1.4, 3.5, and 5.5 shock conditions in order to asses the differences between 2D and 3D flow, and to characterize the pressure attenuation and/or focusing mechanisms. The 2D Mach 1.4 results are validated against published experimental and numerical data, and show energy dissipation by converting the supersonic flow into a subsonic turbulent wake. At Mach numbers 3.5 and 5.5, the array promotes shock focusing and control through the shock structures formed downstream. Comparison of 2D and 3D configurations reveal the 3D geometries offer less resistance due to their increase in effective flow volume, producing higher downstream pressures and more stable wakes, while 2D configurations have nozzle-like exit acceleration. The incident Mach number and effective flow volume are combined to form a dimensionless parameter, the effective Mach number. recent_works.title: Experimental Characterization of Near-Field Recirculation in Swirling Jets Under Freestream and Supersonic Crossflow Conditions
recent_works.abstract: Scramjet engines face challenges in maintaining stable combustion at supersonic speeds due to short residence times. Traditional flameholders introduce thermal loading issues, prompting exploration of swirling-jet flameholders that create toroidal recirculation zones without solid structures. This study characterizes the near-field flow in under-expanded swirling jets, first in freestream conditions and then in a supersonic crossflow. Experiments utilized two resin-printed nozzles (exit diameters 5.5 mm and 11 mm) with adjustable swirl numbers (Sg = 0–1.11) at pressure ratios PR = 5.72–12.7. A self-aligned focused schlieren system visualized flow structures in free jets, revealing that strong swirl (Sg = 1.11) produces unsteady bow shocks and recirculation zones, while moderate swirl (Sg = 0.55) yields stable zones with increasing bow shock stand-off at higher PR. Axial co-flow suppresses recirculation instead of increasing standoff and maintaining the recirculation zone as intended. Laser-sheet Mie scattering provided high-resolution visualization of the near-field jet/crossflow interaction. recent_works.title: Experimental Investigation of Fin-Junction Flow Unsteadiness in Mach 5 Laminar and Turbulent Configurations
GPU-Accelerated Simulation of Flow Over Wing Section With Active Flow Control
recent_works.abstract: We use NekRS, a GPU-accelerated high-order spectral-element large eddy simulation solver, to investigate the separated flow over a NLF(1)-0115 airfoil at Re = 50,000 and alpha = 10 deg. A baseline simulation reveals a laminar separation bubble extending from x/c = 0.079 to x/c = 0.437, with Cl = 1.1034, Cd = 0.0689, and Cl/Cd = 16.07. Spectral analysis identifies two coexisting instabilities: a low-frequency shear layer flapping at St = 0.49 and Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex roll-up at St = 1.57. These frequencies are used to define the forcing parameters for a blowing-only control jet (0.035c slot) positioned upstream of the separation bubble. Six controlled cases are simulated, varying forcing frequency (St_c = 0.49-4.71) and amplitude (A_max = 0.07-0.29) corresponding to a momentum coefficient (C_mu = 0.2%-3.5%). Forcing at the shear layer flapping frequency resonates with the instability and degrades performance (Delta Cl/Cd = -58.9%), while forcing at the Kelvin-Helmholtz frequency and its harmonics promotes earlier reattachment and generates smaller structures that dissipate before reaching the wake.
